appraisal_events.evidence: Bergotte est ce que j'appelle un joueur de flûte... ses livres pèchent par la base... bien mièvre, bien mince, et bien peu viril... plus prétentieux, plus solennel, moins homme de bonne compagnie... un esprit des plus confus, alambiqué.
appraisal_events.explanation: Norpois delivers an extensive, authoritative dismissal of Bergotte's literary work and personal character, calling him superficial, unmanly, and personally vain, locally diminishing Bergotte's standing.

appraisal_events.evidence: M. de Norpois... m'inspira sur ma propre intelligence des doutes plus graves que ceux qui me déchiraient d'habitude... Je comprends mieux maintenant... la mauvaise influence de Bergotte... c'est déjà le même défaut, ce contre-sens d'aligner des mots bien sonores en ne se souciant qu'ensuite du fond.
appraisal_events.explanation: Norpois's confident authority makes the narrator doubt his own judgment, and Norpois explicitly attributes the boy's own juvenile writing to Bergotte's bad influence, locally diminishing the narrator's confidence and literary credibility.

status_effects.explanation: Bergotte's work and person are extensively criticized as superficial, mannered, unmanly, and personally unappealing, clearly diminishing him within this passage.
Norpois's dismissal of an author the narrator reveres provokes graver self-doubt in the narrator than his usual insecurities.
Norpois directly criticizes the narrator's own youthful writing as derivative of Bergotte's superficial style, undermining the narrator's literary standing in the scene.

ambiguities: Norpois's lengthy critique of Bergotte is reported at length in his own voice; within this passage the narrator does not explicitly endorse or contradict it, though the parenthetical about his own graver self-doubt suggests some retrospective distance from Norpois's authority rather than full endorsement.

The passage explicitly separates Bergotte the man from his work ('l'oeuvre est infiniment superieure a l'auteur'), so the blame falls more harshly on Bergotte's person than on his writing, which is treated with somewhat more ambivalence.
